newsitem.title: CANADA: Inco Sudbury workers okay strike mandate.
newsitem.headline: Inco Sudbury workers okay strike mandate.

text.p: Workers at Inco Ltd's Sudbury operations voted on Thursday to give union leaders a strike mandate if a tentative agreement is not reached by the May 31 midnight strike deadline, the union said on Friday.
Union spokesman Gary Patterson said unionized workers at the nickel giant's Sudbury and Port Colborne, Ontario operations voted about 98 percent in favor of the strike mandate.
Patterson said the union called the strike mandate vote because negotiations between the two sides are not progressing.
"It's not going well at all. If I was a betting man I'd be betting we'll be on strike," said Patterson, who is vice-president of union local 6500 of the United Steelworkers of America.
The two sides have been negotiating for about three weeks.
Patterson said the strike midnight May 31 strike deadline was "absolutely inflexible."
The Steelworkers union represents 4,620 workers at Inco's Sudbury mining, smelting and refinery operations in Sudbury and at its Port Colborne refinery.
Patterson said the two sides remained far apart on several non-monetary issues and had not tackled monetary issues.

"The majority of the stuff we're having problems with now are non-monetary, they are issues...that are very important to union values. Things that we will absolutely, under no circumstances, give up."
He said the union struck the company for more than eight months in 1978 to protect its workers on the same issues.
He said the union was in a much better position than during the 1978 strike, when Inco had a 300 million pound stockpile of nickel to fall back on.

"If you do that with a 300 million pound stockpile, you're certainly not going to be too terribly worried about it when there is no stockpile and the price of nickel is good and the company's market share is good and they're selling everything they produce," he said.
Patterson said bargaining would continue through the weekend only as long as progress was being made.

"If the company is still on some of the issues they're on now, I'm sure our bargaining committee is going to say, 'Hey look, come back and see us when you get rid of those things,' and walk away. Because there is no sense in sitting there and arguing about the same things over and over again," he said.
